video_title: Black October! What Is Happening to the Internet?
gist: Security CEOs Hari (Canina) and Odysius (Filix) argue AI agents have collapsed the cost of hacking so that mass scanning and extortion of Web2 and crypto firms is now cheap; offense will dominate for 12-18 months and defenders must attack themselves first.

insights.claim: LLM agents became markedly better at offensive and defensive cyber starting around January, and the cost of running them across many targets has since fallen about 15x on the guest's internal efficiency measure, with a further 10x drop expected every 6-12 months.
insights.speaker: Hari, CEO of Canina Security
insights.so_what: Cyber risk is now an economics problem: attack cost trending to zero implies attack volume trending far higher; favours security vendors and agentic defense spend.

insights.claim: Hacking has shifted from a bespoke, human-expensive skill (weeks of expert time) to a scalable 'factory' that can hit a website for about $10 with no humans, so attackers no longer need to justify ROI per target.
insights.speaker: Hari, CEO of Canina Security
insights.so_what: Long-tail targets (dentists, small SaaS, healthcare) that were previously uneconomic are now in scope; expect broader breach disclosure.
insights.quote: you can build a factory that will like turn in exploits and no humans needed and the economics is falling to zero

insights.claim: The apparent 'Black October' spike is partly a disclosure lag: the guests say incidents have been rising for ~18 months and many of this month's public stories stem from efforts begun about six months ago, so actual activity is running ahead of what is visible.
insights.speaker: Hari, CEO of Canina Security
insights.so_what: Public CVE/incident counts understate the current run-rate; expect headline incidents to keep accelerating.

insights.claim: The CVE publication chart is flat, then sloping, then near-vertical since roughly a year ago, and because of disclosure lag the true current rate is even steeper than the chart shows.
insights.speaker: Hari, CEO of Canina Security
insights.so_what: Use CVE count growth as a leading indicator for demand for patching, pen-testing and AI-security products.

insights.claim: Responsible-disclosure norms are breaking down: once a vulnerability is announced, anyone can point an agent at the affected project (e.g. PHP) and rediscover it immediately, leaving no grace period to patch.
insights.speaker: Odysius, CEO of Filix
insights.so_what: Time-to-patch windows shrink to roughly zero; unpatched open-source dependencies become a systemic risk.

insights.claim: Threat actors are monetizing cheap mass hacking of previously unprofitable targets (e.g. dentists, healthcare) via extortion, threatening to breach or leak unless paid; this is described as a now-scalable cybercrime motion.
insights.speaker: Hari, CEO of Canina Security
insights.so_what: Expect rising ransom/extortion incidents beyond crypto and finance; relevant for cyber insurance loss ratios and healthcare IT security spend.

insights.claim: Crypto was historically the prime target (North Korea funded its missile program via crypto hacks) because payouts were high and on-chain; with attack costs near zero, attacker attention is turning from crypto toward broad Web2.
insights.speaker: Hari, CEO of Canina Security
insights.so_what: Crypto's relative share of attacks may fall even as absolute attack counts rise.

insights.claim: Leaked personal databases enable second- and third-order attacks, such as the Ledger leak from 2021 linked to physical 'wrench attacks' on identified high-net-worth holders, so harm is hard to quantify from the breach alone.
insights.speaker: Odysius, CEO of Filix
insights.so_what: Crypto holders whose identity is tied to leaked data face physical-security risk; privacy/KYC data minimisation matters.

insights.claim: AI agents let attackers combine leaked data and personal context to craft individualized, believable scams at millions-of-people scale, e.g. industrialized elder scams; one engineer's chatbot recited his compensation and partners, showing how much personal data AI products now hold.
insights.speaker: Hari, CEO of Canina Security
insights.so_what: Personalised social-engineering fraud likely rises; AI providers' stored user data is a new high-value target.

insights.claim: A leak of a major bank's records such as JP Morgan's would be a political catastrophe by exposing citizens' finances, illustrating that systemic harm from breaches goes beyond direct monetary loss.
insights.speaker: Hari, CEO of Canina Security
insights.so_what: Tail risk for financial institutions' reputation and regulatory response; the guest frames it as a hypothetical.

themes.theme: Defense posture and the offense window

insights.claim: Offense is expected to dominate for the next 12-18 months, and the recommended defense is to attack yourself with an agentic offensive tool and fix every finding, aiming to raise attacker cost from about $1 to about $10,000, which deters most opportunistic attackers.
insights.speaker: Hari, CEO of Canina Security
insights.so_what: Continuous AI red-teaming is the emerging default security product category; vendors like Canina (Apex) stand to benefit.
insights.quote: if the cost to attack you is like a dollar, like you will get attacked. Like make it like make it like $10,000.

insights.claim: Security will follow software engineering into 'factories': within about two years each company will run a security factory that continuously looks for breaches and proactively fixes them.
insights.speaker: Hari, CEO of Canina Security
insights.so_what: Suggests a shift of security spend from headcount to autonomous agent platforms.

insights.claim: Big-organisation bureaucracy, not missing tooling, is the bottleneck: startups can adopt AI security tools immediately, but large enterprises will be slow, so the whole internet is suddenly a 'dark forest' while security through obscurity breaks down.
insights.speaker: Odysius, CEO of Filix
insights.so_what: Slow-moving incumbents are the most exposed; startups and crypto-native firms have a head start.
insights.quote: you have a tanker a huge ship and you have to turn it while you're being attacked by small speedboats

insights.claim: Crypto firms like Coinbase are better prepared than traditional institutions or retailers because they have lived under constant attack incentives; legacy companies without that pressure are at greater risk, and fiat rails have been exploited before (ATM exploits, Target gift cards).
insights.speaker: Hari, CEO of Canina Security
insights.so_what: Relative security maturity favours crypto custodians over legacy finance; still no room for complacency.

insights.claim: Longer term, agent-written and agent-audited software should be much safer than anything before, but persistent agent attackers mean a world in which one mistake can be fatal; the other guest expects a return to roughly balanced attacker-defender conflict after the 'blood bath'.
insights.speaker: Hari, CEO of Canina Security
insights.so_what: Medium-term vendor demand; the long-term equilibrium is safer code but permanent adversarial pressure.

insights.claim: Individuals should audit which products hold their data and money, ask providers what they are doing about security, and move assets from any provider whose security program has not changed.
insights.speaker: Hari, CEO of Canina Security
insights.so_what: Security posture becomes a competitive differentiator for exchanges, wallets and apps; disclosures could drive flows.

insights.claim: Assume any service will be breached and design for redundancy and limited blast radius, e.g. self-custody with multiple independent devices so several supply chains must fail at once; protocols are also buying orthogonal second-code-base protection.
insights.speaker: Odysius, CEO of Filix
insights.so_what: Demand for independent redundant verification layers in crypto protocols.

insights.claim: Cyber insurance carriers may fail over the coming months: Lloyds warned in 2024 that LLMs would increase cyber risk, yet premiums have fallen consistently since 2024; the guest therefore advises against pure self-custody for the next 12 months and spreading assets across several exchanges.
insights.speaker: Odysius, CEO of Filix
insights.so_what: Watch cyber insurers' reserves and loss ratios; insurance backing of custodians may not be reliable.
insights.quote: probably not self-carling for the next 12 months
